Another $2 million went to Riot's Season 2 qualifiers and championship. The Season 2 World Championship was held in early October 2012 in [Los Angeles, California](/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California") to conclude the US$5 million season. Twelve qualifying teams from around the world participated in the championship, which boasted the largest prize pool in the history of esports tournaments at the time at US$2 million, with US$1 million going to the champions. Locally nicknamed "*La dame de fer*" (French for "Iron Lady") for its use of [wrought iron](/wiki/Wrought_iron "Wrought iron"), it was constructed as the centrepiece of the [1889 World's Fair](/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1889) "Exposition Universelle (1889)"), and to crown the centennial anniversary of the [French Revolution](/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"). Although initially criticised by some of France's leading artists and intellectuals for its design, it has since become a global [cultural icon](/wiki/Cultural_icon "Cultural icon") of France and one of the most recognisable structures in the world.[[5]](#cite_note-Key_figures-5) The tower received 5,889,000 visitors in 2022.[[6]](#cite_note-6) The Eiffel Tower is the most visited monument with an entrance fee in the world:[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7) 6.91 million people ascended it in 2015. It was designated a *[monument historique](/wiki/Monument_historique "Monument historique")* in 1964, and was named part of a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site "UNESCO World Heritage Site") ("Paris, Banks of the Seine") in 1991.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

The tower is 330 metres (1,083 ft) tall,[[9]](#cite_note-9) about the same height as an 81-storey building, and the [tallest structure in Paris](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_and_structures_in_the_Paris_region "List of tallest buildings and structures in the Paris region"). Its base is square, measuring 125 metres (410 ft) on each side. During its construction, the Eiffel Tower surpassed the [Washington Monument](/wiki/Washington_Monument "Washington Monument") to become by far the [tallest human-made structure](/wiki/List_of_tallest_freestanding_structures_in_the_world#Timeline_of_world's_tallest_freestanding_structures "List of tallest freestanding structures in the world") in the world, a title it held for 41 years until the [Chrysler Building](/wiki/Chrysler_Building "Chrysler Building") in New York City was finished in 1930. Tokyo is an international hub of [research and development](/wiki/Research_and_development_in_Japan "Research and development in Japan") and an academic center, with [several major universities](/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Tokyo "List of universities in Tokyo"), including the [University of Tokyo](/wiki/University_of_Tokyo "University of Tokyo"), the top-ranking university in Japan.[[12]](#cite_note-14)[[13]](#cite_note-15) [Tokyo Station](/wiki/Tokyo_Station "Tokyo Station") is the central hub for the [Shinkansen](/wiki/Shinkansen "Shinkansen"), the country's high-speed railway network, and the city's [Shinjuku Station](/wiki/Shinjuku_Station "Shinjuku Station") is the world's busiest train station. Working with fellow economists including [Joshua Angrist](/wiki/Joshua_Angrist "Joshua Angrist") and [Alan Krueger](/wiki/Alan_Krueger "Alan Krueger"), Imbens focused on developing methodologies and frameworks that help economists use a kind of real-life situations known as [natural experiments](/wiki/Natural_experiment "Natural experiment") to test hypotheses about [causal relationships](/wiki/Causal_relationships "Causal relationships"), such as the impact of additional years of school education on earnings.[[24]](#cite_note-24) His frameworks for causal relationships study found use in multiple other fields including social and [biomedical sciences](/wiki/Biomedical_sciences "Biomedical sciences").[[25]](#cite_note-:1-25) It provided researchers with tools to understand the limitations of real-world experiments, improving their ability to better understand the effects of field and [experimental data](/wiki/Experimental_data "Experimental data") based interventions.[[18]](#cite_note-:2-18)

In one of his earliest collaborations with Angrist, Imbens introduced a concept called [Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE)](/wiki/Local_average_treatment_effect "Local average treatment effect") to draw causal inference from observational data. Along with the five permanent members, the Security Council has ten non-permanent members that hold their seats on a rotating basis by geographic region. Non-permanent members may be involved in global security briefings.[[87]](#cite_note-91) In its first two decades, the Security Council had six non-permanent members, the first of which were Australia, Brazil, Egypt, Mexico, the Netherlands, and Poland. In 1965, the number of non-permanent members was expanded to ten.[[88]](#cite_note-92)

These ten non-permanent members are [elected](/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_elections "United Nations Security Council elections") by the [United Nations General Assembly](/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") for two-year terms starting on 1 January, with five replaced each year.[[89]](#cite_note-Current-93) To be approved, a candidate must receive at least two-thirds of all votes cast for that seat, which can result in deadlock if there are two roughly evenly matched candidates. A terracotta warrior from Gansu, with traces of polychrome and gold, from the [Tang dynasty](/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") (618–907)

The historic [Silk Road](/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road") starts in [Chang'an](/wiki/Chang%27an "Chang'an") (present-day [Xi'an](/wiki/Xi%27an "Xi'an")) and goes to [Constantinople](/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") (Istanbul). On the way merchants would go to Dunhuang in Gansu. In Dunhuang they would get fresh camels, food and guards for the journey around the dangerous [Taklamakan Desert](/wiki/Taklamakan_Desert "Taklamakan Desert"). Before departing Dunhuang they would pray to the Mogao Grottoes for a safe journey, if they came back alive they would thank the gods at the grottoes. Across the desert they would form a train of camels to protect themselves from thieving bandits. The next stop, [Kashi (Kashgar)](/wiki/Kashgar "Kashgar"), was a welcome sight to the merchants. At Kashi most would trade and go back and the ones who stayed would eat fruit and trade their [Bactrian camels](/wiki/Bactrian_camel "Bactrian camel") for [single humped](/wiki/Dromedary "Dromedary") ones. After Kashi they would keep going until they reached their next destination.

Located about 5 km (3.1 mi) southwest of the city, the [Crescent Lake](/wiki/Crescent_Lake_(Dunhuang) "Crescent Lake (Dunhuang)") or Yueyaquan is an oasis and popular spot for tourists seeking respite from the heat of the desert. Activities includes camel and 4x4 rides.

There is also data available for Jamaica Plain, just southwest of downtown Boston. This data demonstrates the effects of the sea breeze at Logan Airport, in contrast to that of much of the city of Boston inland away from the coast. Summer daytime temperature records in Jamaica Plain are often higher than Logan Airport by a few to several degrees. Jamaica Plain set a record for the month with the warmest daily maximums in July 2022, with an average daily maximum of 89.2 °F (31.8 °C), while Logan Airport's month of the warmest daily maximums was July 1983, with an average daily maximum of 87.2 °F (30.7 °C).[[138]](#cite_note-NWS_Boston,_MA_(BOX)-138) July 2022 set a record at both Logan Airport and Jamaica Plain with no daily maximum below 79 °F (26 °C) at Jamaica Plain, and 75 °F (24 °C) at Logan Airport for the whole month.[[138]](#cite_note-NWS_Boston,_MA_(BOX)-138) Summers in Boston typically see the yearly maximum temperature climb to at least 93 °F (34 °C), which was Jamaica Plain's yearly maximum temperature in 1996 and 2014; while at Logan Airport the lowest yearly maximum temperature was 91 °F (33 °C), recorded in 1889 and 1996.[[138]](#cite_note-NWS_Boston,_MA_(BOX)-138)

QS also offers universities an auditing service that provides in-depth information about institutional strengths and weaknesses. Called QS Stars, this service is separate from the QS World University Rankings. It involves a detailed look at a range of functions which mark out a modern, global university. The minimum result that a university can receive is zero Stars, while truly exceptional, world-leading universities can receive '5\*+', or 'Five Star Plus', status. The QS Stars audit process evaluates universities according to about 50 different indicators. By 2018, about 20 different universities worldwide had been awarded the maximum possible Five Star Plus rating.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

QS Stars[[59]](#cite_note-59) ratings are derived from scores on in eight out of 12 categories. Four categories are mandatory, while institutions must choose the remaining four optional categories.[[60]](#cite_note-60) They are:

* Teaching
* Employability
* Research
* Internationalization
* Facilities
* Online/Distance Learning
* Arts & Culture
* Innovation
* Inclusiveness
* Social Responsibility
* Subject Ranking
* Program Strength[[61]](#cite_note-61)

Stars is an evaluation system, not a ranking. About 400 institutions had opted for the Stars evaluation as of early 2018. In 2012, fees to participate in this program were $9,850 for the initial audit and an annual license fee of $6,850.[[62]](#cite_note-62)

Armstrong and his first wife, Janet, separated in 1990 and divorced in 1994 after 38 years of marriage.[[214]](#cite_note-214)[[215]](#cite_note-215) He met his second wife, Carol Held Knight, at a golf tournament in 1992, when they were seated together at breakfast. She said little to Armstrong, but he called her two weeks later to ask what she was doing. She replied that she was cutting down a cherry tree, and he arrived at her house 35 minutes later to help. They were married in Ohio on June 12, 1994, and had a second ceremony at [San Ysidro Ranch](/wiki/San_Ysidro_Ranch "San Ysidro Ranch") in California. They lived in [Indian Hill, Ohio](/wiki/Indian_Hill,_Ohio "Indian Hill, Ohio").[[216]](#cite_note-216)[[217]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2005643–645-217) Through his marriage to Carol, he was the father-in-law of future [New York Mets](/wiki/New_York_Mets "New York Mets") general manager [Brodie Van Wagenen](/wiki/Brodie_Van_Wagenen "Brodie Van Wagenen").

In May 2005, Armstrong became involved in a legal dispute with Mark Sizemore, his barber of 20 years. After cutting Armstrong's hair, Sizemore sold some of it to a collector for $3,000 without Armstrong's knowledge or permission.[[218]](#cite_note-218) Armstrong threatened legal action against Sizemore unless he returned the hair or donated the proceeds to a charity of Armstrong's choosing. Sizemore, unable to retrieve the hair, donated the proceeds to charity.[[219]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2012628-219)[[220]](#cite_note-220)
